description: 6/8 ist ein offline gegründetes Team von Erstsemestern der TU Dresden.
summary:
Our Project 6/8 is an interactive tool that identifies and characterizes new terrestrial analogs for lunar bases and landing sites. Using open NASA and ESA data, we compare Earth locations with lunar reference sites such as the Shackleton crater rim. For each location, we calculate a similarity score from features, including terrain (NASADEM, Copernicus DEM, LRO LOLA), surface temperature (MODIS, LRO Diviner), surface properties (MODIS albedo, ASTER GED) and vegetation and precipitation (MODIS NDVI, GPM). The results are shown on a map that ranks candidate sites and explains where they match and where they differ.

Existing analog sites such as Devon Island’s Haughton crater are not fully characterized. Our data-driven method makes the selection of test sites transparent and repeatable, and highlights a number of additional candidates e.g. in Mongolia, China etc.. This helps mission teams test equipment and methods on Earth before flying, making future lunar missions safer and better prepared.
details:
What it does and how it works
Project 6/8 finds and characterizes terrestrial analogs for lunar bases and landing sites. The user selects a lunar target, for example shackleton crater, and the tool compares it with locations on Earth. For each feature, we calculate a similarity score s = 1 − |x_Earth − x_Moon| / (x_max − x_min), where x is the feature value and x_max and x_min give the range of that feature. The overall score is a weighted sum S = Σ wᵢ · sᵢ over [N] features. The results are presented as a map that shows the best matches and where each site differs from the target.

Features: terrain (NASADEM, Copernicus DEM, LRO LOLA), surface temperature (MODIS, LRO Diviner), surface properties (MODIS albedo, ASTER GED), vegetation and precipitation (MODIS NDVI, GPM) and imagery for visual comparison (Sentinel-2, LROC, Worldview).

Benefits
The method is transparent and repeatable. Instead of relying on a few well-known sites, mission planners can compare many candidates with the same criteria and see why a site ranks high. Weights can be adjusted to the mission goal, such as rover testing or habitat design.

Intended impact
Better characterized analog sites help teams test equipment and procedures on Earth before flying, which reduces risk and cost for future lunar missions. The approach relies only on open data, so researchers and students can reuse and extend it.

Tools and software
Programming languages, e.g. Python; mapping tools, e.g. L MapLibre; data access via NASA Earthdata Search, NASA PDS and the Copernicus Data Space Eosystem; visual checks with NASA Worldview; hosting, e.g. GitHub Pages; presentation made with PowerPoint. Hardware: standard laptops.

Creativity
We turn the question “where is similar to the Moon?” into a measurable score instead of a qualitative list. We combine NASA Earth data with lunar reference data from LRO and show differences next to similarities. We tried to give a nicely visualized overview and were experimenting quite a bit with various features. The Lack of programming knowledge was a factor we tried to balance out through the usage of some supportive AI tools. But we tried to make it as accessable as possible so even people that are not familiar with the topic at first are able to understand it and gain something from it.

Factors we considered

  • Data coverage: NASADEM does not cover areas north of 60°N, so we used Copernicus DEM for sites such as Devon Island and Svalbard.
  • Different resolutions and dates between Earth and lunar datasets by using various formulas.
  • Normalization of features so that no single feature dominates, and the choice of weights.
  • Limits of analogs: Earth cannot reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum or radiation, so a high score means similar terrain and surface conditions, not identical conditions.
